speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgiil (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL-REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR EDMONTON WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have a question of privilege arising out of a question of privilege raised last evening at ten o'clock by the hon. Member for Edmonton West at a time when I v/as not-and I apologize for this-in the House. In that statement the hon. gentleman, I think, misled the House as to the attitude I had taken earlier in the debate, and also I think misled the House as to his own attitude in the matter.
I should like to read very briefly, sir, from what the hon. gentleman said; I will not read all he said:
During the course of my remarks I was questioned by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgiil) as to the first occasion on which there had been an appeal, under Standing Order 26, from Mr. Speaker's ruling. On that occasion the Minister suggested that the appeal had come from the official opposition.
Well, Sir, I made no such suggestion. I would draw hon. Members' attention to Hansard, page 1638, where the hon. Member for Edmonton West accused us on this side of the House, because we had later voted in an opposite sense from the sense in which we had voted on the occasion to which he referred when he was Speaker, in these words:
Not only was that an exercise in hypocrisy, it was cynical.
I interrupted him and asked who made the appeal on that occasion. I asked because I did not know who made it and I was seeking information. The hon. Member went on:
It was contemptuous and it was contemptible. It was cynical in that it was repeated on a number of occasions.
Then, Sir, the hon. Member went on in his question of privilege to say:
I would like to clearly point out that the appeal came from the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Douglas) and that he was ably abetted in that appeal by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The date was given as June 17, 1963, and I have looked up the record. It is true that although the right hon. gentleman has sought to move the adjournment of the House, the appeal was taken by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and the appeal was put to the House. I have here the Hansard for June 17. I have the list of those who voted for the appeal, who voted in a manner which the hon. Member for Edmonton West has characterized as hypocrisy, cynicism and contempt of Parliament, and I find in the list of those who voted the ex-Speaker of the House, the hon. Member for Edmonton West.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL-REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR EDMONTON WEST
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL-REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR EDMONTON WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Minister of Transport has sought to clarify the record further, I will say there was no attempt at all to confuse the issue. In this question last night the Minister indicated where the appeal had come from and I endeavoured to reply, and it is to that I limit my reply.
So far as the question of the appeal was concerned, I do recall that I gave way to a rather temporary degree of annoyance on the occasion. I regretted the decision, and I think I apologized to Your Honour privately for what I thought was perhaps a wrong gesture on my part on that occasion, for which I accept full responsibility and which I hope I will never repeat.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING FOOD LABELLING
speechtext:
Representations have been received by the Department of National Health and Welfare from officers of Allergy
May 26. 1965

Questions
Information requesting that the labels of all food products carry a complete list of ingredients.
The organization has been informed that the problem with respect to the sensitivity of many people to certain food ingredients and the need for listing ingredients on the labels of all food products are under active study by the Food and Drug Directorate. The matter was also referred for consideration to the Advisory Council of Consumers at a meeting held at Ottawa during February of this year. The members of the Council agreed that more information should appear on food labels but that the process of revision should be a gradual one. They felt that the whole allergy problem should be investigated with a view to determining the number of allergy sufferers in Canada and ascertaining the ingredients to which people are most frequently sensitive. This information is now being gathered by the Food and Drug Directorate and it is hoped that an early and practical solution to the problem can be found.
Changes have been embodied in the Food and Drug Regulations during the past year to require more complete listing of ingredients and more informative labelling. It is expected that, as time goes by, the number of foods exempted from a list of ingredients will be reduced and that many of the standardized foods will require an ingredient list on the label.

speechtext:

Negotiations are under way with the vehicle manufacturers to extend to all civilian departments vehicle repair arrangements similar to those established some years ago for the Department of National Defence. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF MAIL PRIVILEGES FROM "NATURAL ORDER" ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
On May 11, Mr. Speaker, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), I said that an investigation was being conducted to determine whether the printed matter distributed by an association called "Natural Order" and whose address is 1630 Alberni Street, Vancouver 5, B.C., was such that it should be denied the use of mail facilities.
First, I wish to thank all members who gave me the co-operation I requested by sending me documents which they found reprehensible. Thanks to this help, officers of my department, in co-operation with those of the Department of Justice, were able to determine that certain documents from this so-called "Natural Order" association were of such a nature that no normal person could help but consider them as hate-spreading literature.
Having heard the opinions of my advisers, there is no longer any doubt in my mind that the distribution of such matter through the Canadian mail constitutes an infraction. Consequently, I ordered today that the use of the mail be refused from now on to David Stanley, the association known as "Natural Order" and to any person, regardless of his name and address, who might be implicated in the distribution of these offensive publications.
My order is provisional and Mr. Stanley will be duly informed that he can appeal therefrom. If he does, his appeal will be heard in the usual manner by a board of revision which, after considering the evidence, will recommend on my initial action, that is whether the provisional prohibition order should be revoked or whether it should be made final.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Olson:
That this House recognize the need for improving its proceedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1. That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 36 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions "That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair"; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year. That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-two members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
House of Commons Procedures
2. That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.-

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a long speech and I do not claim to be an expert on this question, but I should like to make a few remarks concerning this proposed change in certain parts of the standing orders of the house.
I should first like to point out to the house that it is rather surprising to see that it is those who abused the most the rules of this house who today want to change those rules. In this respect, one has only to recall the abuses of those who are now sitting on the front benches, for instance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), his colleague and former minister of justice, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), the Minister of Transport (Mr. 1678	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures Pickersgill) who have all literally abused the privileges of the house, more particularly during the 1962 session. They are the ones who, today, would like to prevent present members of the opposition from having their say in the house.
It will be recalled that on the question of unemployment, so often debated in the house, your predecessor in the Chair had to call the present Secretary of State for External Affairs to order, but that he and his colleague, the present High Commissioner in London, with unqualified boldness, challenged time and again the Speaker of the house.
In the study of this proposal one cannot but find that it is a package, if you will permit me the expression, a very nice package containing something which is surely quite astonishing, in spite of all the precautions taken to advise the house on the various procedural changes that were intended. Now, those changes have but one purpose, according to me, and that is to bring in some form of closure rule, a gag of some kind. And everybody finds it revolting that, in 1965, the government could have such a measure accepted.
It is the duty of the opposition to examine closely and study down to their finest details the legislation and proposals put before the house. I am firmly convinced that what the government is after in the proposal now before us is a method by which it can be sure of having the closure rule accepted.

Mr. Speaker, since our group has already made its views known concerning the changes in the standing orders and since we also intend to support the new amendments to be moved by the government, X merely wish to say a few words about the staff, that is the reporters and interpreters, who will have to remain on duty at meal-time, if the proposed amendments are accepted, while the members will be able to have their meals or perform other duties.
I appreciate that it is necessary to get on with the business of the house which is ever increasing and getting more important, but I feel that the services provided to the house by our devoted and efficient staff should be kept in mind and that it is essential to think about these people before imposing this extra work on them.
If it is utterly impossible to allow the staff of the house to get away at meal-time, it will be imperative to increase substantially the number of employees so that their situation becomes a little more human.
Mr. Speaker, considering that sessions now last 15 to 16 consecutive months, considering also that most employees had to work in the House of Commons continually for a period of about six to eight months a year, we can realize the extra work that this may involve; that is why I would like to warn the government against this situation so that it may right now start recruiting competent and devoted employees. Incidentally, I may say that it is certainly possible to find here, in Canada, competent people, without having to look for them in other countries.
In my opinion, it will be necessary to increase the salaries, make advertisements if necessary, in brief, spend the money necessary to attract more competent people, before going in other countries to seek employees for the House of Commons.
House of Commons Procedures
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call your attention to another small matter. I want to warn you against the fact that the question period will be shortened.
The opposition does not seem to have raised a great deal of objection to the proposed amendment, but in my opinion, the Speaker will have to look toward the opposition side rather than the government side because if government members were to ask questions for 30 minutes, the opposition members would have no opportunity to ask any.
However, should this happen, protests would surely be raised by the opposition, which is ready to co-operate with the government so long as government members co-operate with the opposition. At any rate, I am convinced that Liberal Members will be able to have their questions answered by getting in touch directly with the ministers concerned without having to go through the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few remarks I wanted to submit to you and I hope that the government will take them into consideration.

I have always felt that the Minister was lucky who got his bills on at the very end of the session, when people were tired and perhaps the bills went through with almost no debate. That is not the way we should do our business. What we are seeking to do by this whole scheme is, not to reduce the amount of time for debate but to provide for the orderly use of the time that is available. If we are going to function effectively-and here again the hon. I think it will be recalled that on two occasions in the House when we voluntarily put limitations on supply, toward the end of last session and once on an earlier occasion, on both occasions the Government did have in those estimates a novel item which was not a true supplementary; and on both occasions those items were withdrawn because it was felt it would be an abuse of the rules of the House to attempt to do anything of a novel character without proper and adequate debate. I do not think the same consideration applies to the same degree with what might be called true supplementaries. I take the familiar example where you have voted $50,000 for a wharf and you need about $3,000 more to complete it; the House has already approved the wharf, and there is hardly a great matter of principle involved in the estimating that has gone into it, unless it is, again, something inordinate. These two objectives are not easy to achieve. I think we all recognize, especially those of us who have had the opportunity of sitting on both sides of the House, that the two objectives are not too easy to reconcile.

Let me repeat that over and over again the threat has been made that unless we accept the throttle an election is going to be proposed. We are not going to be intimidated in that way. Let that be absolutely clear and definite. We have endeavoured to do everything we can to bring about changes in the rules in keeping with the preservation of those things which are necessary to parliamentary rights. It is because of that attitude that in all sincerity I advanced the idea of a non-partisan Speaker, but the reply given by the President of the Privy Council was nothing else but a gratuitous sneer. He said, "Why don't you pick out the Deputy Speaker because he has a small majority". We do not choose Speakers on the basis of their majority, large or small.
We have as Speaker a man long in Parliament, a man of fairness, courtesy and consideration. He will not always be right; no Speaker can be. Sometimes he will be on the wrong side in an argument but we know that the present Speaker will never be on the side

of wrong. I advanced this idea because of the need to assure the maintenance of the proprieties in the House, so that those people who trampled on parliament in 1956 in the pipe line debate will not again be placed in a position where they can deny that which they did at that time when they disgraced the institution of parliament. We want to be sure that is not going to happen again and that our rights are not going to be sacrificed.
I made this proposal in all seriousness, but what was the answer of the President of the Privy Council? He spoke in a condescending manner, but at the very same hour the Prime Minister was stating in Sudbury that the matter would receive consideration and that there would be communication with the Speaker to ascertain the facts. The President of the Privy Council spoke one way and the Prime Minister, with more responsibility and respect for Parliament, spoke the reverse.
In so far as this section is concerned, we come back to this question. Does this Government want to have a Parliament that is effective? If it does, then never have we been closer to the general acceptance of a permanent Speaker than today. That is the feeling of people across the country. Why not accept that? If it is accepted, we will go a long way in the acceptance of the curtailment of those things that are traditionally the rights of parliament, provided we are assured there will be no repetition of the pipe line debate when all the rules of parliament were torn up, when the leader of the C.C.F. of that day, Mr. M. J. Coldwell, rushed up to the mace and when parliament was in a shambles because those sitting opposite at that time, who today again occupy the seats of Government, destroyed those things which can never be repaired. There are a number of them sitting over there today and we want to be sure that their activities in the pipe line debate will not be repeated.
In so far as the section dealing with the examination of the estimates is concerned, an exception has been made in the suggestion put forward by the Minister of Transport. That goes part way. If he is in that spirit, I suggest that the Government should also accept a reasonable number of supply motions I think that at this time six supply motions are unnecessary, provided we have the assurance of a Speaker who will carry out the proprieties and the traditions of parliament in such a way that all of us will realize that they are being observed. I ask this question. Is there anything unreasonable in asking

If we are going to have six, then in the interest of bringing about that orderly debate that the hon. gentleman mentioned I would be prepared to see the debate on such motions reduced to one day. However, in this House we have a multiplicity of parties and such a move might deny some of them the opportunity to place the views of their respective parties before the House.
Will the Government agree to add to the suggested amendments an exception covering four periods for motions to go into committee of supply? If it will, this in large measure will attain the objectives that the Minister had in mind when he expressed himself so forcibly a few minutes ago and at the same time would preserve the traditional right of the Opposition to move amendments to motions to go into supply. Acceptance of this proposal is not asking too much. The Minister of Transport has already shown a desire to bring about changes in a spirit of conciliation and not to browbeat parliament into the acceptance of something that is unjust. That being so, I make the suggestion that if there is the acceptance of that comparatively minor addition, we in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, would be prepared to accept No. 14, Section 1, with the changes that have been suggested by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).

I have often said, and I know it will be quoted back to me, that the time spent on the study of estimates is sometimes wasted time because we take item by item. We get bogged down on a certain item, as the Minister said, and more important ones receive less attention. Everyone who has had the responsibility of Government knows that by the simple course of exhaustion estimates that do not receive full examination are sometimes passed through the House in the last days.
In the United Kingdom, the course followed is not to take item by item. The course followed is to have a pound item, or whatever the nominal amount may be, in respect of each department of government, and then there is a concentration in the discussion on the weaknesses or injustices that have happened during the year, or any suggested changes for betterment in the year ahead. All of us have seen how often there are

Frankly, as I have listened to the arguments and read Hansard, I believe that the idea of sending estimates to committees will be beneficial. It will be beneficial to the Members of the House. I should like to speak to the subamendment. In so doing, I should like to indicate our attitude toward the suggestions made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) when he spoke earlier this afternoon.
May I say at the outset that he is quite right in saying that our attitude is not one of take it or leave it so far as our amendment is concerned. He is quite right in saying that the amendment I proposed on behalf of this party the other day was not one that we insist must be taken in its entirety. We are bargaining for the best possible arrangements. However, I must say to the Minister of Transport that what he asks us to do, in our
1686	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures view, is too much. May I take a moment longer to emphasize the fact that we are coming at this whole question as Members of a party that wants to see improvements made in our procedures? When we say we want to see improvements made, we have in mind in particular the whole question of the best use of our time. We, therefore, accept the proposition that it makes sense to decide on some kind of over-all limit with regard to the time we spend on estimates.
In this connection, I may say that I listened, as other Members did, with a great deal of interest to the speech made last night by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) in which he made a case that is delightful to make for what one might call unlimited free speech. This is something we all believe in, and we would all defend it to the death. The only thing I feel I must say to my neighbour from Winnipeg South Centre is that the desire for unlimited free speech has to be balanced with the need to reach a decision, the need to reach a conclusion on some questions so that we can get on with others. I think he would agree with me that the whole problem of parliamentary procedure is trying to find that balance.
I suggest that the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre has seen the light with regard to that balance, so far as estimates are concerned. He is an advocate of unlimited free speech but at the same time he is prepared to accept an over-all time limit so far as the amount of time spent on estimates is concerned. We are talking the same language so far as this part of the motion is concerned. Like the Leader of the Opposition, I regret that we are not in Committee of the Whole so that we might have a much freer discussion of these questions. But I hope that even with Mr. Speaker in the Chair we can agree on a formula so far as the time for estimates is concerned.
The Minister of Transport asks us on this side of the House, and in this party in particular, to withdraw our amendment on the understanding that the Government would move an amendment, the terms of which he read out a while ago. May I say that we cannot do that, for reasons which I shall give in a moment. However, this does not mean that we are totally unwilling to withdraw our amendment if a more acceptable counterproposal can be offered by the Government. The Government's first motion contained the proposal that there should be an over-all time limit on supply of 36 days in a session. It was indicated, for the purpose of supply, that in

DEBATES	May 26, 1965
those 36 days four categories of business would be considered. The first was the 12 days that might be spent on motions that Mr. Speaker leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply. The second was the main estimates; third, interim supply, and fourth, supplementary estimates. We stated, in the remarks I made on behalf of this party last Thursday, and in our amendment, that that is going too far. We are prepared to accept the 36 day limit, but included within those 36 days should be only main estimates and interim supply. We think that the 12 days possible when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair should be excluded, and so should supplementary estimates.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We are making progress with regard to supplementary estimates. I am prepared to accept the refinement in the subamendment moved by the hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), which is mainly to the effect that a supplementary estimate of $3,000 at the back of the book, which is to be added to the $50,000 at the front of the book, be called within the 36 days. I think the Government has seen our point that additional estimates brought in at the end of the year or after the main estimates have been approved, should not be included in those 36 days.
We think we have reached agreement on this but, Mr. Speaker, it is still our view that motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply are a different kettle of fish altogether. Merely to call them motions having to do with supply and then to call estimates supply, and to say that both are the same kettle of fish, is playing with words. When we are in Committee of Supply dealing with estimates, whether main, supplementary or interim, we are dealing with estimates; but when we are debating motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair, even though it is to go into Committee of Supply, we are on something which is much more akin to the Debate on the Address in Reply to the Throne Speech, or to the Budget Debate.
Usually these motions are amended and become non-confidence debates. They are in a category completely to themselves and we do not think they should be included with the days that are spent in Committee of Supply. Hence we feel that the Government should give consideration to what I think is the pith of my amendment, namely that there should be a separation of the motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair from all the other ways in which we deal with supply.
May 26, 1965	COMMONS
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a suggestion a moment ago, and I wondered if he had been experiencing some osmosis himself, when he suggested that the number of supply motions in a session be reduced to four from the present six. We would go along with that. As a matter of fact in certain quarters we have proposed that very change, and we are glad he agrees with us. This would cut the time on these debates from 12 days to eight days. But we still think that having done that, those eight days should be outside of the days allotted to supply itself. The way the Leader of the Opposition put it a moment ago was that it would be eight days outside of the 36. In those terms, even that 36 might be negotiable. For example, I might settle for 35; but do not push me too far. The point is that the quantities in this respect are one thing; the principle is another.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. Member a purely factual question. I do think what really matters from the Government's point of view is what the total number of days is. If the Opposition felt they would like to have more time on estimates by dropping one of the supply days it would have that extra day, whereas if these things were in two separate compartments they would not be transferable from one to another.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is not osmosis but the Minister must have seen the few notes I made while he was speaking because I was going to come to that very point.
I suppose my hon. friends to the right will want to throw in a gibe or two, but let me put it this way. If there were only one Opposition party, and particularly if we were that party, there would be no problem. But there are four Opposition parties, and the fact that one Opposition party passes up a supply motion in order to have more time for estimates in Committee of Supply is no guarantee that the other parties will not take up that day, and we would be in the position, all of us on the Opposition side, that we might want to follow a certain course but any plans we would make would be thwarted by decisions made in other groups over which we have no control.
I suggest that it would be far better in principle to have these motions outside the
DEBATES	1687
House of Commons Procedures time proposed. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) says it makes no difference to the Government, but I still ask him to consider the difference in principle between the kinds of debates we have. In Committee of Supply we are dealing with estimates, but on motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair we can discuss anything under the sun, and it is usually whatever the Official Opposition decides will be the subject for non-confidence on that particular occasion.
I may say that in a manifesto for parliamentary reform which this party put out some time ago, we suggested this whole practice might be reviewed, that maybe instead of nonconfidence motions being attached to motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply we could have just one motion in a session for Committee of Supply, and then have provision for a number of occasions in a session when Opposition parties might ask for, and get, a one or two day debate on subjects when they arise.
The trouble with the present arrangement is that we get these debates when the Government decides to go into supply, and the Opposition has to decide what is wrong at that particular point. It might be far better if the Opposition could pick the times when subjects should be brought forward. But I am just emphasizing the fact that this is something completely different from the consideration of estimates, namely the debate on motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply.
I am as co-operative as I can be. I am just as co-operative as the Minister of Transport.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Or the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
I want to see this rule worked out so that it will work, but the Minister is asking too much if he asks me to withdraw the principle of my amendment, which is that the debates on the motions for Mr. Speaker to leave the Chair must be separated from the time allocated for consideration in committee of estimates themselves.
I think we have reached an accommodation on the question of supplementary estimates. I think in all quarters of the House we are agreed on this. We are agreed in all quarters, I believe, that there has to be an over-all time limit on estimates themselves, and I hope the Government will see the
May 26, 1985

House of Commons Procedures justice and the principle of what we are asking for on this point.
I have refrained from suggesting any precise quantities, other than in the proposal that the number of supply motions be cut from six to four. I think this could be done quite easily. On the first we could enter ten departments, on the next two five each, and on the fourth all the rest. We would all be satisfied to make that change. Whether the 36 days should be changed to a figure like 35 is something which is still negotiable, but it does seem to me this is the way to get a rule regarding supply that will be acceptable to the House, and that will work. That is what we want in parliamentary reform. We do not want something that seems to have been handed to us by fiat. We want something we have worked out in discussions among various Members and parties in the House. I think we can do this. Therefore I ask that the Minister of Transport withdraw his request to me to withdraw my amendment, until some other proposal has been made. There are lots of Ministers over there who still have the opportunity to speak and make other proposals. If one comes up that seems to meet common agreement the Government can be assured we will give it favourable consideration.
While I am on my feet I would like to say a few words about another point, and I do so at this time because Your Honour is in the Chair and if I sit down I cannot get up again unless another amendment is moved at some stage. The other point I wish to mention concerns paragraph 2 of item No. 14 on the order paper, which deals with the allocation of time. I spoke at some length about this the other day and indicated our general approval of the principle of allocation of time. I also indicated our approval of the main outlines of the proposed rule set out in Standing Order 15A, but the one phase of 15A which bothers us most-and there are several little details we should like to change, but they are not as important-is that contained in subparagraph 5, namely the situation under which the Government, even though it has been beaten four to one in the Business Committee, can still come back in the House and effect its will if it has a majority of support for the motion it makes.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I recognize that there are certain precautions. I recognize that it takes practically a calendar week to put the provisions of subparagraph 5 into effect. I recognize that a

government is hardly going to go through that week's process unless the matter is serious, unless public opinion is behind it, and unless the issue is the kind in respect of which the government feels it could carry it to the country. However, I still feel that it does not add up for a government to be able to go to the Business Committee with a proposition and be beaten four to one there, but still be able to come back to the House and effect its will.
Various precautions might be considered in this regard, and one would be that instead of the choice being related to a unanimous vote, or just allowing the Government to have its own way, there could be a provision for a unanimous vote, such as we now have, or a provision for a majority vote. It would seem to me that if in the Business Committee there was a majority of three to two, since we now have five parties, that is a condition in respect of which it might be appropriate to have a day's debate and let the House make a decision.
Another precaution might be to provide, as I indicated last Thursday night, that on the last day of an allocated time period, under this rule, the adjournment hour should be lifted so that Members who feel they have something they wish to say would get a chance to say it. By doing that we would admittedly give up the right to filibuster in respect of that particular item, but we would be protecting the rights of Members who feel they have a contribution to make, even though they might have to sit here half or all of the night to do so.
I think also the kind of precaution that could be written into paragraph 5 could relate to some kind of absolute minimum below which no order could be moved. It seems to me that some reasonable time- three or four days per stage, or something like that-might be acceptable so that guarantees of that kind could be put into or added to paragraph 5 of the proposed Standing Order 15 A.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I make this suggestion as one who favours the principle of time allocation. I go along with my hon. friend, the Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), in his defence of the rights of Members to speak, and I go along with him in the defence he made last night in respect of those occasions during which Parliament can by lengthy debate prevent a Government from doing something that is vicious or scandalous. I also feel that the other side of
May 26, 1965	COMMONS
the coin must be looked at, because we have to balance the right of unlimited right of speech and the need for discipline so we can have the kind of situation in which we can deal with all the issues that come before us. It is my concern in respect of a time allocation that there be time for us to deal with the multifarious issues and problems which face us.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that before we finish with item No. 14 on the order paper the Government will not only come forward with an acceptable counterproposal so far as paragraph 1 is concerned, which has to do with time spent on estimates, but will also come forward with an acceptable amendment to subparagraph 5 of proposed Standing Order 15A as set out in paragraph 2 of the resolution.
In relation to both these matters, namely time spent in the committee on estimates and time spent under an allocation, I still feel that the Government is not as impressive as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) thinks it is when it talks about the extra time we are going to get. The Minister told us that what the Government was doing was not cutting down the time for estimates, but giving us more time. I have seen the figures which he says the arithmeticians have worked out, but as I look at them, I am reminded of the information that has been given me to the effect that within the last ten or 12 years, excepting the sessions that ended in dissolution, the total amount of time spent on supply of all kinds was something of the order of 190 hours. We have been given the figures in hours rather than in days for an obvious reason.
We are told that as a result of the rule changes the Government is proposing we will have 198 hours, and that therefore we are being given more time. That suggestion is made on the assumption that the extra time we will have between six o'clock and eight o'clock will actually be extra time used for the consideration of estimates. As I said before, I am afraid that many of those hours will be spent by hon. Members keeping the House going while others go for a meal, and I question the logic of the Minister of Transport when he said earlier today that perhaps there was something in the point I made about its not being desirable to discuss legislation between six and eight, but perhaps we could spend that time discussing the estimates. It seems to me there is a hint there that the estimates are not quite as important

In the earlier part of the session we have no guarantee that the estimates will be available for discussion between the hours of six and eight, particularly if we are going to accept the idea, which I think is a good one in respect of which we are all in approval, of referring estimates to committees. The estimates will be before those committees for some time and there will likely be a few weeks during the early part of the session when the estimates will not have come back from committee for discussion in Committee of Supply. So, even with the best will in the world, we will not be able to discuss the estimates and make constituency speeches between six and eight o'clock, and we will likely be dealing with Government legislative items.
All I am suggesting is that the Government is oversimplifying the matter when it suggests, with a little simple arithmetic, that we will get more time under a time limit than we have without a time limit. Perhaps that is another issue we should deal with when we are considering item No. 15 on the order paper. Perhaps at that time we can deal with the question in respect of committees. Perhaps then we can also deal with the question of appeals from Mr. Speaker's rulings and the suggestion of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) regarding a permanent Speakership.
The only comment I want to make at this time in this regard is that I think an issue of this kind regarding the Speakership, particularly if one is talking about a person to fill that position, should be discussed among the parties or among the leaders rather than
1690	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures here. I do not believe that one Member of Parliament, no matter who he is, should stand up and endeavour to name the individual who should be appointed as the first permanent Speaker of the House of Commons. I do not think that is the way to get at that particular problem.
These questions of committees, appeals and the other matters, including the extended sittings between the hours of six and eight, are more related to order No. 15 than the item which we are now discussing, and perhaps we should wait until we are considering that item to discuss these matters. However, I thought I should mention the points I have made, so as to make clear the point that we are putting forward, namely that the Government is not going to add as much time as it thinks it is by this time extension.
I rose at this time to indicate our willingness to co-operate and our willingness to listen to counterproposals, but at the same time I must make it clear that the counterproposal of the Minister of Transport is not adequate to persuade me to withdraw my amendment. I should like to suggest that the Government should come back with another proposal or, and this is the simplest way to do it, accept my amendment and take supply motions out of the 36 day limit. However, Mr. Speaker-and I think this has already been said-I agree there is something in the point made by my hon. friend and others, namely that it would require some alteration to the proposals in the resolution in regard to the form of the motion to be put to the House, if that is required, and we should take into consideration some of the points that have been made. Reference has been made to the desirability of having a permanent Speaker. I am not quite sure what we mean by "permanent Speaker"; there has been no definition, that 22620-109
House of Commons Procedures I know of, of a permanent Speaker. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

speechtext:
That, of course, does not depend necessarily at all on the tenure of office of the Speaker. But if we do that, and indeed if we do not, then whatever rules we make to increase the efficiency of the House and the better conduct of public business may not be as successful as we may like them to be; because it is important that the Speaker should not only be independent, but it should be obvious that he is independent and he should be freed from pressures against his independence. I have tried to make that clear whenever I have spoken on this subject. Since we are to strengthen the independence of the Speaker, a very effective way is to make it impossible to appeal his rulings. I cannot think of any better way of strengthening his independence. That has been accepted in other legislative assemblies. It does not do very much to strengthen the independence of the Speaker when his rulings in two years, as they were in 1962 and 1963, were appealed on 23 occasions-and the appeal was upheld on only two occasions.
Surely, however the Speaker may be appointed, however long he may be in the chair, if his rulings are going to be appealed 23 times in two years, his authority is going to be undermined.

speechtext:
I said the other day, from 1957 to 1962. I was not corrected at that time. If I am wrong, I will be glad to make the correction. It was a five-year period. This is one way to strengthen the independence of the Speaker. Another way of strengthening his independence-and I just throw this out as a suggestion-is to ensure that in some way after he ceases to be Speaker-and if we took steps to see he was Speaker for a longer period of time than is the case at present, this would be even more important-we could, by pension or otherwise, make him financially independent. In other words, Mr. Speaker, he should be made financially independent in some way after he has discharged his duty to the House of Commons.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It is very important, then, that strengthening the independence of the Speaker is a matter of agreement. It will have to be done by agreement between the parties; I do not think it could be done by any formal act of the House, although I may be wrong in that. But it can be done by agreeing that the Speaker who is appointed will be appointed on the understanding that he will not be opposed by any party in a subsequent election, if he is available to continue as Speaker. That is one way of establishing what we now rather loosely refer to as a permanent Speakership.
I can see a good deal of merit in that, and I said the other day when we were considering this matter that when a Speaker is chosen it should be on the understanding that he would not be opposed at the next election. I can think of the present occupant, a man of fairness and objectivity, as being the kind of person to whom we should like to give that assurance if he were available; and there certainly is no evidence to support the suggestion that he would be available for the next parliament. I can think of the Deputy Speaker as being the kind of man to whom we on this side of the House would be very glad indeed to give that assurance.

If these two Members of the House, who have conducted the affairs of the House with fairness and impartiality, were not available, then I can think of no man worthier or more qualified to be given this assurance that he would not be opposed if he became a Member of Parliament and acted as Speaker than former Mr. Speaker Michener; and I am very glad to put his name forward in this connection as a man we would be very glad to see in the Chair under the conditions I have mentioned, if Mr. Speaker and Mr. Deputy Speaker were not available themselves.
I was very glad to get confirmation of the feeling from the other side of the House in respect of the two Members I have mentioned, and the third, who I think we will all agree was one of the most effective Speakers this House has ever had. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should give consideration to the advisability of helping industry finance the capital works necessary to minimize pollution of water and air caused by industrial wastes; this financial help to take the form of special depreciation allowances on equipment and installations provided for the above purpose.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to induce the Government to provide special depreciation allowances to industries for works they instal to control the problem of water pollution and air pollution. The budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) a few weeks ago took that very action with respect to water pollution. The problem of air pollution is to be studied by the Council of Resource Ministers next year and, with the lead taken in this field and the precedent established in the case of water pollution, I am sure that when they have dealt with the problem of air pollution we will probably have recommendations leading to similar action. Because action has already been taken with respect to water pollution and is likely to be taken with respect to air pollution, I would respectfully request unanimous consent of the House to withdraw my motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal of the pulp and paper industry to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) was really caused by the strong line that has been taken by the Ontario Water Resources Commission which has set deadlines for the pulp and paper industry and other industries by which time they must have the pollution caused by their operations in check, or punitive measures will be taken. The scale of this can be interpreted either grandly or narrowly. To my knowledge there are some 29 pulp and paper mills in Ontario in 27 different locations, I believe. The scope of the pollution they cause varies tremendously.
As a matter of fact, in the Prime Minister's constituency there is a mill at Espanola which has perhaps the most difficult problem of all. There is a mill at Dryden in the constituency of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson) which is notorious throughout that whole region because of the fact that by its method of disposing of its waste it has in a sense ruined a couple of good fishing rivers and lakes and has been a blot, if you like, upon the whole region. I am talking about specific locations and these are good examples.
In my own riding, where there are four pulp and paper mills and a couple of others so close to my riding they might almost be said to be in it, the problem is different. For example, Marathon on the north shore of Lake Superior has a more serious problem in this regard than Kimberly-Clark at Terrace Bay. I understand that the Ontario Paper Mill at Welland has a particularly difficult problem if it is going to clear up this whole matter.
May 26, 1965

There is another problem involved which has not been straightened out at all and it comes into play when you go beyond the question of the mechanical clearing up of pollution. Who bears the responsibility for the continuing clean-up? I can give an example of this. Suppose at Espanola the pollution is blocked by sewage means, by various pits, pools, screening and so on. What about the consequences that have spread far beyond the actual mill site? Who is responsible for these, and is it possible that some tax concessions or depreciation allowances on the part of the Federal Government should be brought into play?
It is my understanding that the general attitude taken by the Department of Finance is that they will give so much in terms of depreciation allowances, but no more. They will not go so far as to give the kind of allowance that is given in the case of research expenditures. It is my understanding that any company that spends so much money on research gets 150 per cent in terms of a depreciation allowance for that expenditure. In other words, there is built into this kind of expenditure a really large incentive.
The main reason I quarrel with the hon. Member's interpretation of what has been done is that this particular aspect has not been dealt with. It is my understanding, an understanding gathered from personal representations I have made to the Minister, that this has not been met by the Minister of Finance. He and his department have not been prepared to go that far. Yet it is important that it should be considered for this reason. There are no rules you can pull out for any particular pulp and paper mill and say that if they do this it will end pollution. There is no absolute way that a pulp and paper min superintendent can say that they will spend so much and instal so much equipment and this will abolish the pollution. To quite an extent the whole field is still very experimental.
It is quite possible that the mill at Espanola might spend $11- million on various pollution treatments and still not be successful. It might still be under the gun. In other words, there is in prospect the possibility that much of this expenditure might not be effective. We are not absolutely sure just what are the best engineering and technical steps to take in order to clear up pollution.
There is another point involved. You really cannot generalize from one pulp and paper mill to another. After all, a mill located on a body of water the size of Lake Superior
Financial Aid to Minimize Pollution has a greater tolerance in what it can release into the adjoining waters than a mill situated on a smaller lake or river such as the mill at Espanola or the Abitibi mill at Sault Ste. Marie.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I am concentrating particularly on the pulp and paper industry, but it seems to me it is the one that is most important in the initial stages in Ontario and other parts of the country as we move toward clearing up pollution. In the pulp and paper industry we are getting, particularly in the boreal forest area in Quebec, Ontario and Northern Manitoba, a development on the logging side that is the most promising thing we have ever had in connection with our streams. I refer to the transition that is happening very rapidly, the disappearing tradition of having your wood moved to the mill by water. As a consequence, we are not going to have the problem of sinkage and of barkage that has been so fatal in many of our streams, particularly in Quebec, with regard to trout fishing. This is one thing that is being cleared up by the transition to mechanical logging and the integration of logging operations to the necessity for the industry cutting down its inventory, and having its inventory tied in much more closely to the daily, weekly or quarterly operation plan.
We are getting an advance on the woods stream side from a point of view of the raw material going into the mill, but in so far as the mill problems are concerned there is no pattern from mill to mill; there is no pattern in terms of location, of the amount of pollution that the area or the waters can absorb. It is impossible to be absolute about what expenditures will achieve in the way of blocking off pollution. I want to see the ukase of the Ontario Water Resources Commission respected. I want to see it achieve its objective. I am very much aware also of the fact that we have an industry that is healthy, but there is a certain delicacy in the balance, particularly with some mills that might be called marginal. All of us who have industries relating to pulp and paper, as I know you have, Mr. Speaker, are aware of some of the problems that are involved, particularly because of the price of newsprint and other paper products for producers on the West Coast. It is a matter of common knowledge that there are several mills and locations, communities, in Ontario and one or two in Quebec in which the future, in terms of expansion or continuation, because of rap-
May 26, 1965

Financial Aid to Minimize Pollution idly rising wage costs and other factors, is not really so good.
It is possible if that kind of mill, that kind of operation, is presented with extremely large anti-pollution expenses, that could tip the scales toward pulling the whole operation down or cancelling it out. It is for that reason I think the Department of Finance, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), should go further and offer this special kind of depreciation so that the expenditures are classed as experimental research, at least in part. I think this would be a move of great encouragement to the pulp and paper industry. I just could not allow this particular motion to go through from the point of view that the whole thing has been solved by what has been given in the budget.
I was not aware we were proceeding with this motion. I was informed we were going to proceed with the motion in the name of the hon. Member for Carleton (Mr. Francis), so I could not get my material over here. However, I hope the House will accept my word that I have material from the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association; I have material from Kimberly-Clark, from several of the Abitibi mills and from a couple of other pulp and paper companies, which indicate that, delighted as they are with the move that was made in the Budget announcement, they still feel that this other aspect should have been considered. So far as they are concerned, they are still open to it, they are still making representations. Certainly I, as one of the Members from a region affected by this problem, consider it is still open. It was for this reason I felt I should make these remarks.
There is one last point I wanted to touch upon before I sit down. There are many Members here, certainly some of them in the House, from areas in which pulp and paper is not a major industrial factor. They may be saying, is this not some kind of special consideration for particular industry in a particular location? Is this not going against the grain with relation to what tax incentives should try to do, that is have a general rather than a specific effect? I can grant the merit of that argument. I know I have always felt when I have been sitting here listening to special pleas for special interests that do not relate to my own part of the country, that this may be wrong. Sometimes when these special pleas are made, as they have been in the past, for such things as acreage payments, you sometimes feel one particular part of the country is getting an advantage

through perhaps stronger lobbying or more political pressure whatever the case may be. In this particular case the hon. Member who sponsored the motion recognizes that we are dealing with a conception that is an ideal; we have an ideal of clean air and good pure water in this country. It is an ideal that we, in our hurry and the haphazard way we have gone about developing things in the past generation, have tended to destroy. Remedial measures are very much necessary, but I do not feel you can lay responsibility on any specific industry or any specific location. It seems to me that all of us and our forefathers bear a responsibility for the way pollution has come into being in so many parts of the country.
It is because the Ontario Water Resources Commission, in a sense, has isolated the problem and has come up, through the powers given to it by the Provincial Government, with the ability to dictate and direct remedial measures that this kind of resolution has been brought forward. It is not just pollution from pulp and paper mills. You get pollution from so many different kinds of organizations and from municipalities themselves. It seems to me that the Department of Finance and those agencies in the Government that are interested in research-I think particularly of the National Research Council, the Water Resources Branch in the Northern Affairs Department, the Department of National Health and Welfare and its whole attitude toward air pollution and its merging and mixing with the problem of air pollution- should come up with a policy.
I think hon. Members know that the resource ministers are preparing to deal with this, not in a policy way but in a fact-finding way. We are having symposiums this year and next year, and there is going to be a very large conference in October, 1966, that will touch on this problem. With this kind of situation ahead of us, we need some policy interests; we need the continuing support of people like the hon. Member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) and the hon. Member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who also has views in this regard. We need them to keep prodding the Government inside and externally, too, to come up with something more imaginative than we have. I suggest that the hon. Member's motion should be voted upon and approved by this House. I am somewhat disappointed that he would feel, although perhaps it is natural in a way that a Government Member likes to glory in the things a Govern-

Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the withdrawal of the notice of motion as suggested by the hon. Member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn), but I am afraid I cannot overlook the opportunity to welcome the hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) to the ranks of those of us who defend private enterprise, he having argued that taxpayers should aid the private enterprise operators in the pulp and paper industry to eliminate the pollution of air and water. I had not intended to speak on the motion this afternoon, but when I found the subject was being opened up, despite the hon. Member for Broadview's desire to withdraw it, I decided I would like to make references to a point or two.
The air and water of this country belong to the people of the nation, and not to private individuals or private companies. They belong to the people as a whole. It strikes me as peculiar that we should be thinking of asking the taxpayers of Canada to help finance the correction of polluting agents that industry is using in the manufacture of its products.
In the Province of Ontario, particularly in the major municipalities, we have continuous inspections going on all the time against air pollution caused by too much smoke. This applies not only to industry but to railway steam engines and other engines putting out a lot of smoke into the air. Does this motion mean that the taxpayers should be expected to finance the conversion of industry in the control of a smoke nuisance which, after all,
Financial Aid to Minimize Pollution is pollution of the air? Why should not these industries be expected to govern their actions in some manner so that they are not polluting the heritage of the people of pure water and air? There are laws against what industries can dump on the streets, in order to keep the streets clean. Why should the taxpayers of the country be expected to aid in clearing up the pollution that private industry is creating?
The fact that many of these mills are in unorganized territories have given them all almost a carte blanche in their own minds to pollute the water and the air of those territories. I am thinking of some pulp and paper companies in Northern Ontario in the midst of woods on the sides of swift flowing streams, in unorganized municipalities, and they are of the opinion that no law of God or man applies to them. Some of them are trying to work seven days a week, and that is why I say they think the laws of God should not apply to them.
I believe the Government-and when I say Government I mean federal, provincial and municipal-should demand that private industry conduct its operations in such a way that they do not pollute the heritage of the people, pure air and pure water. I am not in 100 per cent agreement with the idea of taxpayers giving money to help a poor, hard-driven industry to correct the situation it is creating.
The hon. Member for Port Arthur has referred to the plant at Espanola. I taught school in 1922 in the town of Massey, Ontario, where the Sauble joins the Spanish River. I am familiar with the Spanish River back 150 miles from its mouth, and I know it was polluted originally by lumber mills letting dead head logs flow down it, and throwing bark into the stream.
The same thing has been done in the past to the Ottawa River by the great lumber barons of this area. This discussion does not apply just to pulp and paper mills. Lumber mills were allowed to pollute the water in the first place, and I do not believe that the taxpayers should be asked or expected to help finance the correction of an original mistake made by the manufacturers themselves.

We have laws that a new plant must be installed with the most modern techniques. I know of many cement plants that have to have dust suppressors, and these are very costly. Many municipal power plants must instal cinder suppressors, and these too are costly. All this is part of the cost of doing business, and if the cost of removing the effluent from any industrial process is too costly, then it is an uneconomic process.
It is the same as if you were going after buffalo hearts and you killed all the buffalos to have the hearts and then threw away the carcasses. Bringing it up to modern times, it is the same as if you were going after beef liver and you killed all the cattle to get the liver, and then threw the carcasses away. As a matter of fact our laws today insist that older established industries bring themselves up to date. They are given a period in which to do so, and I believe this is fair.
When we talk about air pollution let us not load it all on the back of industry. In cities like Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal where the majority of winter heating is by oil, as com-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in my capacity as the Member for Coast-Capilano as we also have a pollution problem on the west coast.
The hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said that the Government should show some imagination in respect of pollution control. It has shown some imagination, I believe, in respect of the control of pollution of the nation's waters. I should like to see that same imagination applied to the control of pollution of our air as well. In other words, I should like to see the two-year fast tax write-off which, according to the current budget, applies to water pollution, extended to air pollution as well.
I understand the Government does not as yet have a complete picture of the total cost to the federal treasury of such a measure, namely a measure to control air pollution or assist in controlling air pollution by a fast tax write-off, but I hope that as soon as this information is available it will move in this direction, presumably through the medium of the budget.
Pulp mills have been mentioned as major offenders in respect of water pollution. Pulp mills and chemical plants are also major offenders in respect of air pollution. The Federal Government has limited authority regarding the matter of pollution. This is a matter largely for provincial control. Obviously, however, through the fiscal measures open to the Federal Government, it can encourage projects which would help to clear up our air, as well as our water.
I should also like to see encouragement through research grants, and in this respect I agree with the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). Research should be aimed at improved methods-cheaper plant and equipment in other words-for cleaning up the nation's air as well as our rivers and streams. The pulp and paper industry is having a difficult time, as it happens, regarding odours emanating from kraft pulp mills. It is very difficult to remove the last vestiges of odour from the air, particularly from the effluent from kraft pulp mills. A great deal of research has already been carried out in various parts of the world in this respect, but equipment which can remove all of the odour from the effluent is immensely expensive. Therefore I think a second prong to this attack, and an even more effective approach to it, would be assistance in the form of grants in respect of research.
I hope that the pulp and paper industry, through its trade associations and research
Financial Aid to Minimize Pollution institutes, will combine in tackling this problem. It certainly would be encouraged to do so through Government assistance to the industry, with the grants administered perhaps by the Department of Industry, specifically directed toward the removal of pollutants in the air.
I would not want to wait until the Resource Ministers conference, and I believe this would require more than one, to tender their final recommendations in this connection before attempting to do something. I am sure the Resource Ministers will bring a great deal of information to bear on this subject, but as usual, they will tend to collect facts, prepare data sheets, giving us a host of technical information while at the same time continuing to pose the policy question: What is to be done about this very difficult problem.
Certainly I should like to see the Federal Government make a move in respect of air pollution through a fast tax write-off as has been done in respect of water pollution. I should also like to see it devote more funds to air pollution control through co-operative arrangements with the Pulp and Paper Research Association in an effort to find a solution to this problem of air pollution.

It is quite possible that it is economically impractical for institutions such as hospitals to use only natural gas, which the hon. I do say, however, that certain pollution does not emanate from private industry, and I do not think it is the sole responsibility of the private aspects of our economy to remove all pollution. I might also point out that this is one case where there would have to be a retroactive effect of the legislation, with which I do not think most Members would agree. Some of these elements of pollution were brought into the economy by private industry at a time when they were perfectly within their legal rights to use the kind of equipment which caused the pollution. grey areas in our constitution which for so many years has been bedevilled by the fact that in a very difficult and costly procedure such as this, as between federal and provincial authorities there has been a tendency to say, "Well, it is the other fellow's responsibility". I think it is one of the things that disturbs all of us who are Members of this House, that we do not seem to tackle these very great, essential and permanent problems in our body politic and our economy. They are put by the wayside, when it is obviously the most important thing in Canada today, surely, to use what is left of our natural resources better than we have in the past. The question of water, the question of pollution and the question of the use of our natural resources are areas which must be covered by both federal and provincial legislation if we are going to achieve in these areas a better way of life in the future than we have in the past.
In the Province of Ontario, while they wield the big stick through the Water Resources Commission, to which our friend from Port Arthur has referred, they do very little about providing any of the finances or any of the incentives that the Federal Government has tried to do here. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if there is one body of people for whom it is inequitable to bear the cost, it is the home owners.
I suggest this is one area that should be solved at the higher levels of government through a broad basis of taxation such as the provincial and federal governments have. It is to be hoped that the Conference of Resource Ministers will soon attack this problem boldly, forthrightly and pervasively, on a Federal-Provincial basis, through cooperative federalism, so that we can pass on to those who come after us pure air and pure water, which was our bequest from the past.

Having started off by asking to have it withdrawn, having then entered into a debate, I wind up in the rather unique position of a Member single-handedly and with malice aforethought apparently talking out his own bill. I listened with interest to the comments made on the motion and probably it might have been helpful, had I known that this would develop into a debate, for me to put on the record an explanation why I put the motion as I did. I think that while much of what has been said I would agree with, many people have missed the purpose I was trying to achieve with this particular motion.
Let us look at the problems we really face. The thing I am concerned about is the critical, pressing problem we have in certain parts of the country with pollution of our water resources. I consider the problem serious enough to say that action is required not two, three or four years from now, but right now. I think steps have to be taken and taken quickly.
Bearing that in mind, where does the responsibility lie? Water is a provincial resource and therefore the legislative responsibility generally rests with the provinces. It is up to the provinces to enact the legislation which is necessary to clean up the situation. Where does this pollution come from? It comes from two major sources. It comes from industry and it comes from municipalities: industry in terms of its waste products; municipalities in terms of the sewage they discharge.

With that background, with the tact that this is a provincial matter, with the fact that urgent action has to be taken, with the fact that it can only come from two sources- with these facts in mind it seemed to me important that we get these two sources stopped right away from further polluting our waters. In other words, we must stop industry from dumping pollutants into the streams and stop municipalities from doing that as well. Only the provinces can enact the legislation to bring this about; but in the Province of Ontario there is very good legislation, legislation which is being enforced. I think this is a tribute to the Provincial Government, even though it happens to be that of a party I do not support. It is a good piece of legislation and a good program.
But industry which has been allowed to go on for a number of years using or wasting our resources, and has never been called to account for this, cannot suddenly find the money necessary to make the expenditure required to clear this problem up. We have allowed industry to go on in this way. We have allowed it to play by a certain set of rules and we have now started to change the rules and enforce that change of rules. I felt that if industry was to meet these new rules, industry needed help, and the best help I could think of was a form of tax concessions on special plant and equipment it would need to put in to do the job. This is exactly one of the measures contained in the Budget. I am very glad to see it is contained in the Budget because I think it will now enable industry to live up to the legislation the provinces must pass quickly, before it is too late in critical areas of the country, in order to stop additional pollutants going into our waters.
The hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) suggested that this was not enough, and I could not agree more with the hon. Member. I think I have made two speeches in the last few months in the House on pollution, and to me it is obvious that this in itself is not the sole answer to the problem. To me this is the shock treatment necessary for the immediate, critical areas of the country so that they can solve the problem facing them. Beyond that there is much which has to be done.
We have the secondary problem of sewage coming in from municipalities. The provinces must get after the municipalities and must insist that the municipalities put in the proper sewage treatment plants, so that they do not dump pollutants into the waters. If the provinces will do this, and if the provinces

or the municipalities need financial help from the Federal Government in terms of loans, then it is up to the provinces and the municipalities to come to the Federal Government and request such assistance. There is already on the statute books assistance for sewage treatment plants under the National Housing Act. It also seems to me that the provisions of the Municipal Development and Loan Act did provide low interest loans to municipalities so that they could have the funds necessary to go after their end of the problem. I think these two steps in themselves, however, are still not the complete answer.
The problem of research was raised. A good deal of research must be done. Research must be done by industry so that industry knows what type of plant is the most efficient to treat its effluents so that it can find the best method of stopping pollution through its waste products. Over and above that, research is required by Government agencies- the sort of research being carried on in a very limited way, unfortunately much too limited, by the Great Lakes Institute. They are doing research, but should be doing much more research, as should other agencies, to determine how much pollutant a given body of water can take, what are the flow characteristics, the currents and so on, how much you can dump into bodies of water without destroying them. We have only scratched the surface in this area; much work remains to be done here.
The hon. Member for Port Arthur mentioned the problem of residual effects. Take, for example, a stream which has been polluted for years and years and years. If you stop industry or a municipality from dumping further pollutants into the stream, there still remains a good deal of damage which has been done over the years. Who has to come back and repair that damage? We do not know the answer to that question. I would be happy if this were the only problem we had to solve, namely how to clean up streams which were once polluted but are no longer. I would be delighted if that were the only question which we faced. Some day we will have to face this very question.
As I see it, this is really a matter of provincial concern, but it may not be. At the present time we do not know the answer to that question.
